questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] cached values that outlive the code that wrote them (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/06). Scenario: a release changes the shape of the product DTO kept in the shared cache (v2 splits the price into amount plus currency and renames one field); the rolling deploy takes about 45 minutes, during which 12 pods running a mix of v1 and v2 code read and fill the same shared entries, which carry a 300-second TTL; on day 2 a regression forces a rollback, so v1 writers return while v2-shaped entries are still cached; and the product lookup also caches 'not found' for 10 minutes, which is how a product created one minute after a failed lookup stayed invisible. Write your design before you look: how a reader knows which shape an entry has, a version in the key versus a decoder that accepts both shapes, what the cache does at deploy time and at rollback, what an entry a reader cannot decode turns into, whether and how not-found answers are cached and what clears them, and how you prove each of these in tests. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] An entry's shape is part of what the key must say: a key states which requests may share one representation, and a v1 reader and a v2 reader do not share one. Put a shape version in the key namespace, built by the single key function both sides already use, so the two code versions fill and read disjoint entries for the whole rollout.
[w2] The existing scheme already leaves room for this: the key the worked trace stores carries a v1 segment, so a new shape is a new namespace rather than an overwrite of old bytes.
keyPoints.quote: The read path stores the value under `bazaar:v1:store:s1:product:canvas-market-tote`

keyPoints.text: [w3] A versioned key moves the problem to invalidation: an edit made on a v2 pod clears the v2 entry, but the v1 entry for the same product is still served by v1 pods until its TTL, so during the window every invalidation has to clear the key of each shape still live, or one fleet half shows the old price.

[w3] If you keep one key and decode tolerantly instead, the cache boundary gets an explicit compatibility policy: a new optional field gets a justified default, an entry missing data the reader requires is rejected and reloaded from the source, and an old-shape fixture stays in the test suite beside the new one.

[w3] An entry a reader cannot decode is a miss, never a 500: catch the decode failure at the cache boundary, count it, load from the source of truth and (if this reader owns the shape) overwrite. The chapter's review question about an unavailable cache applies equally to a cache that holds bytes this binary cannot read.
keyPoints.quote: What happens when the cache is down?

keyPoints.text: [w2] Rollback is designed before rollout: the release that first writes v2 must be preceded by one whose readers already accept v2, so the version you would roll back to never meets an entry it cannot read; that is the cache's form of the N-1 rule migrations follow.

[w2] Not-found answers get their own, much shorter TTL and a writer: the create path clears the not-found entry for the new item, or not-found is not cached at all, which is the honest choice the pulse key resolver made by never storing unknown keys.

[w1] The proofs are sequence tests through the real key function: seed the cache with a v1-shaped fixture and expect a v2 read to reload rather than throw, and look up a missing product, create it, and expect the next lookup to find it.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — rollout week on the same design: thirty minutes into the 45-minute rollout, the remaining v1 pods start failing every product read with a deserialization error; the next morning the rollback brings v1 writers back while v2-shaped entries are still cached; a merchant deletes a product and re-creates it under the same handle, and it keeps answering 'not found'; and someone proposes flushing the whole shared cache on every deploy from now on. What breaks, how do you see it, and what is the repair?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The v1 failures are old code meeting new bytes: compiling the new DTO changed nothing about the decoder still running in old pods. The repair is a runtime fallback at the cache boundary (an unreadable entry becomes a reload) shipped before any writer emits v2, or a versioned key so old pods never see v2 at all.

[w3] With one shared key, the rollback turns the entry into a tug of war: v1 writers refill it in the old shape, any v2 pod still serving fails on it, and each side keeps overwriting the other. With versioned keys the rollback is quiet, as v1 pods go back to their own namespace.

[w3] A quiet rollback can still be a stale one: if the store behind the cache drops its TTL argument, the v1 namespace still holds the values it had the day before, and rolled-back pods serve day-old prices as hits. Verify that the store expires entries before relying on the old namespace having emptied itself.

[w3] The re-created product stays invisible because a not-found entry can only be keyed by what was asked for, the handle: there was no product id to tag it with. The write side speaks product ids, so creating the product clears nothing, and the stale 'not found' lives out its full TTL. Create must clear the handle-keyed negative entry explicitly.

[w2] The tell is an invalidation that touched nothing: the tag invalidation reports zero keys and still returns success, so count zero-key invalidations on create and alert on them, alongside a per-version counter of entries that failed to decode.

[w2] A flush on every deploy trades a rare correctness bug for a guaranteed load event: the design method's worksheet arithmetic puts a warm cache (95% hits) at 50 origin reads a second out of 1,000 and a cold one at all 1,000, and a flush makes every pod in the fleet pay that cold rate at the same moment, on every release.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your choices against the alternatives: a shape version in the key versus one key read through a decoder that accepts both shapes, flushing the shared cache at each deploy versus letting both code versions read side by side, a short TTL on cached not-found answers versus clearing them when the item is created versus never caching them, and shipping readers ahead of writers in two releases versus one release that changes both. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A version in the key means no reader ever meets a shape it does not know and a rollback needs no cleanup; the price is a cold set for each shape during the rollout, roughly double the entries, and invalidation that must name every live version. A tolerant decoder keeps one warm set, but its compatibility code lives until the last old entry is gone, and a decoder bug corrupts reads quietly instead of missing.

[w3] A flush at deploy start does not even buy what it promises on a rolling deploy: old and new code run together for the whole window, so v1 pods refill old-shape entries right after the flush. Side-by-side reading (versioned or tolerant) is the only option that covers the overlap; the flush only adds a cold start.

[w3] A short not-found TTL caps how long a new item stays invisible and still shields the source from repeated lookups of missing ids; clearing on create gives instant visibility but only works if the create path can name every negative key; not caching misses is correct by construction and sends every miss to the source. A cached negative answer is replayed to every caller until it expires, the same replay hazard a stored failure creates in an API idempotency store.

[w2] Readers first, writers a release later, costs a second deploy and a short period where the new shape is understood but never written; one release that changes both is faster but leaves no version you can roll back to safely, so rehearse the rollback with the cache populated in the new shape before choosing it.

[w2] Every option here answers the same question about the copy: when the code that wrote it changes, who can still read it, and for how long. The TTL bounds how long an abandoned shape lingers, so a rollout plan states it.
keyPoints.quote: A cache is a second copy of the truth with a delay.
